rationale: The BNA proceedings contain the full P-W082 poster abstract and a separate pattern-glare hallucination study. P-W082 classified 24 Parkinson participants with hallucinations and 26 without, plus 13 controls, and compared attention-task performance and computational drift rates. The later paper analyzed different denominators. The poster reports group status and perceptual processing without a dried fig exposure or a visual episode-rate comparison.

The pathology review distinguishes neurodegenerative diseases using disrupted proteins, cell populations and diagnosis-specific tissue findings. The Lewy body disease section treats visual hallucinations as a clinical feature. There is no measured food intake or episode-frequency comparison.

The early Parkinson ICICLE-PD imaging analysis compares resting functional connectivity by cognitive impairment status and against controls. The discussion explicitly reports no visual hallucinations in the PD-MCI sample. The study addresses connectivity, not a dietary intervention or the course of hallucinations.

The review distinguishes formed visual hallucinations, passage and presence phenomena, visual illusions, pareidolia, later loss of insight and delusions. It summarizes earlier clinical and imaging studies without enrolling a new comparison. No dried fig intake analysis links to these outcomes.

The practical delirium review discusses onset, inattention, fluctuating alertness and visual or auditory screening. Its diagnostic examples separate acute delirium from persistent Parkinson psychosis. It does not measure a culinary exposure or Parkinson visual episode frequency.

The study transplanted neural progenitors into the striatum of immunodeficient transgenic mice. It reports post-transplant motor, learning and tissue outcomes. Hallucinations appear in the human phenotype background; the animal experiments have no dried fig exposure or visual hallucination count.

The Parkinson cognition review surveys mild cognitive impairment, dementia risk and visual hallucination status in longitudinal cohorts. Its visual hallucination discussion cites earlier observations of disease progression. It supplies neither a food comparison nor a new estimate of visual episode frequency.

The authors examine cortical RPT6 and proteasome activity in donated brains from Parkinson dementia, Lewy body dementia, Alzheimer disease and controls. The correlations include cognitive disease measures. Clinical visual hallucinations are background features, without an exposure analysis or frequency endpoint.

The review compares imaging biomarkers used across idiopathic Parkinson and atypical parkinsonian syndromes. It distinguishes diagnostic visual symptom features from PET and MRI findings. It has no measured dried fig exposure or Parkinson visual episode outcome.

The SGIM supplement contains a separate anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis case with visual hallucinations and a severe vitamin B12 deficiency case with imbalance. Their diagnoses, treatments and outcomes differ. No member links a measured dried fig exposure to Parkinson visual episode frequency.

This review describes psychiatric and movement manifestations of Niemann–Pick disease type C, with visual hallucinations discussed in its differential diagnosis. It does not compare a dietary exposure or episodes in idiopathic Parkinson disease.

The mechanistic review compares aggregation and interactions of amyloid beta, tau, alpha-synuclein and TDP-43. It mentions visual hallucinations to characterize dementia with Lewy bodies and Parkinson dementia. Its comparisons concern tissue pathology and model findings, without food intake or visual episode rates.

The resting-state fMRI meta-analysis compares the coordinates of reported case–control activity changes across 28 between-group contrasts. Its focus is consistency of intrinsic brain function across Parkinson imaging studies. It does not compare fig intake or visual episodes.

The clinical imaging review discusses amyloid and tau PET alongside characteristic cognitive syndromes, including the visual hallucination phenotype in dementia with Lewy bodies. This is a diagnostic imaging synthesis with no culinary exposure or Parkinson visual episode-frequency contrast.

Ten Parkinson patients and sixteen controls underwent visual evoked magnetic-field testing. The Parkinson participants reported neither hallucinations nor visual impairment. The visual cortical response and nonmotor measures are pre-hallucination physiology rather than a test of food intake or visual episode frequency.

The presynaptic dopamine imaging review separates specified visual hallucination status from auditory outcomes and other nonmotor measures. Table 4 compares imaging reports and notes limitations such as baseline cognition and medication related hallucinations. It contributes no new dietary or visual episode-rate comparison.

The age-stratified comparison reports memory, executive and visuoconstructional tests in 202 participants with dementia with Lewy bodies and 236 with Alzheimer disease. Visual hallucinations are a diagnostic phenotype discussed alongside cognitive results. The paper gives no Parkinson dried fig exposure or visual episode-rate comparison.

The multicenter study examines the MRI swallow-tail sign in 97 participants across dementia, mild cognitive impairment and control groups. The imaging sign concerns nigrosome visibility, while visual hallucinations appear among clinical features of Lewy body dementia. There is no dried fig exposure contrast or visual episode count.

The clinicopathological review differentiates dementia syndromes by clinical features and the distribution of protein aggregates. It describes recurrent visual hallucinations as a diagnostic feature of Lewy body dementia. It does not report a dietary intervention or Parkinson visual episode-rate comparison.

The diffusion tensor imaging meta-analysis combines 39 neuroimaging studies involving 1,855 participants. Its extracted outcomes are fractional anisotropy and mean diffusivity across regions. Visual hallucination status in individual subgroup descriptions does not supply a dried fig or episode-frequency comparison.

The prefrontal-cortex proteomics study selects 19 dementia with Lewy bodies, 21 Parkinson dementia and 21 control brains from a larger pool. It compares protein abundance and synaptopodin. It does not measure dried fig intake or visual hallucination frequency.

The unilateral dopamine-depletion rat study compares gait and regional glucose metabolism with lesion severity. It cites visual hallucinations as human context for visuospatial circuitry. The rat outcomes provide no dietary comparison or measure of visual episodes.

The cannabinoid review compares different receptor-active drugs, cannabis preparations and trials across Parkinson motor and nonmotor outcomes. Adverse-event reports include visual hallucinations, while the underlying trials concern chemically distinct exposures. The review supplies no dried fig or visual episode-frequency result.

The bicentenary essay surveys the history of Parkinson disease, its pathology and neurological symptoms. Visual hallucinations appear in a synthesis of perceptual and neuropsychiatric circuitry. The essay does not measure dried fig intake or compare hallucination episode rates.

EANM member OP-367 compares PET patterns by visual hallucination status in dementia with Lewy bodies. The full 838-page proceedings and rendered member boundaries distinguish the imaging features from clinical symptom counts. Singular fig tokens are figure labels. No member measures dried fig intake and Parkinson visual episode frequency.

The postmortem study measures copper, iron, manganese and zinc fractions by Parkinson tissue region and disease group. The expected higher iron and lower copper are concentrated in the soluble substantia nigra fraction. USDA documents all four minerals in dried, uncooked figs. That food composition bridge is indirect. The brain study measures neither dietary intake nor visual episode frequency and supplies no claim direction.

The study compares temporal states of functional brain connectivity in 31 people with Parkinson disease and controls. Its visual hallucination discussion cites earlier visual-processing work. The actual outcomes are MRI network patterns and clinical association measures, with no dried fig intake or measured visual episode rate.

The case describes reversible secondary parkinsonism with a dural arteriovenous fistula and reports absence of visual hallucinations in its differential discussion. Vascular treatment and clinical movement change are separate from Parkinson dietary exposure.

The Johns Hopkins cohort uses occurrence and remission of a broad DSM-IV psychotic disorder in idiopathic Parkinson disease. Its repeat visits distinguish diagnosis changes and medication changes, without an isolated visual episode count or measured dried fig intake.

The South London study compares hospital admissions in 194 patients with dementia with Lewy bodies and 776 matched Alzheimer patients. Its discussion points to a separate visual hallucination research program. Admissions and costs are the evaluated outcomes, without fig or visual episode-rate data.

The Parkinson biomarker review discusses clinical symptoms including visual hallucination status and measures including imaging and nonmotor markers. It does not evaluate an edible fig preparation or visual symptom episode rate.

Two patients with secondary parkinsonism from dural arteriovenous fistula had hallucinations during their vascular illness. Their timelines include symptom improvement following embolization, a recurrence after the first procedure in one case, and medication changes. There is no idiopathic Parkinson dietary comparison.

The smartphone motor study compares waking function with end-of-dose measures in 92 Parkinson participants. Table 2 reports visual hallucination histories in 8 of 20 people with measured morning motor benefit and 26 of 72 without (P=.797). The separate history item is prevalence, without a dietary exposure or serial visual episode count.
